mcqs.question: A language model correctly completes "If it's raining, you should bring an ___" with "umbrella" at high probability. What does this demonstrate about next-token prediction as a training objective?
options: The model has a separate reasoning module distinct from its next-token prediction mechanism
Predicting the next token well often requires implicitly learning grammar, facts, and causal patterns, since all of these influence which word is actually likely to come next
This particular completion proves the model has true causal understanding of weather
Next-token prediction only works for factual completions, not causal ones
mcqs.explanation: The point of the example is that next-token prediction, as a plain statistical objective, forces a model to internalize patterns that look like grammar, facts, and basic causal association purely because those patterns are what make next-word prediction accurate — there's no separate reasoning module (A is false), and this doesn't establish deep causal understanding, just that the pattern is statistically learnable (C overclaims). It's not limited to factual completions only (D is false — the umbrella example is itself a causal-pattern completion).

mcqs.question: A trigram language model assigns zero probability to a grammatically valid, plausible three-word phrase simply because that exact trigram never appeared in training. What problem does this illustrate?
options: Overfitting to the validation set
The sparsity problem — most possible n-grams never appear even in a huge corpus, so pure count-based estimation assigns zero probability to many valid, unseen combinations
A bug in the tokenizer that fails to recognize valid words
The vanishing gradient problem
mcqs.explanation: This is the defining weakness of count-based n-gram models: combinatorial vocabulary growth means the vast majority of possible n-grams are never observed in training, however large the corpus, so naive counting assigns them zero probability regardless of how plausible they are. This isn't overfitting (A, a different failure mode), not a tokenizer bug (C, the words are recognized fine individually), and vanishing gradients (D) is a neural-network training issue, irrelevant to count-based n-gram models which have no gradients at all.

mcqs.question: An RNN-based language model performs noticeably worse than a Transformer-based one at capturing a dependency between a word near the start of a 200-token document and a word near the end. What best explains this gap?
options: RNNs cannot process sequences longer than 200 tokens under any circumstances

RNNs must propagate information sequentially through every intermediate time step, causing long-range signal to degrade (vanishing gradients); Transformers let any token attend directly to any other token regardless of distance
Transformers use a larger vocabulary than RNNs by design
RNNs and Transformers have identical long-range dependency handling; the difference must be a training bug
mcqs.explanation: This is the central architectural gap language modeling exposed: RNNs carry information forward step-by-step, so a dependency spanning 200 steps has to survive that entire chain, typically degrading via vanishing gradients; Transformer self-attention connects any two positions with one direct computation regardless of distance. RNNs can technically process sequences of that length, just with degraded quality (A overstates it), vocabulary size isn't the differentiator here (C is irrelevant), and this is a well-documented architectural difference, not a bug (D is false).

mcqs.question: Model A has a lower perplexity than Model B on the same held-out test set, using the same tokenizer. What does this most directly indicate?
options: Model A is definitely a larger model than Model B
Model A consistently assigned higher probability to the actual next tokens in the test set than Model B did, indicating a better statistical fit to that held-out text
Model A necessarily produces more factually accurate outputs than Model B
Model A was trained on more data than Model B
mcqs.explanation: Perplexity directly measures how well-calibrated a model's predicted probabilities were against what actually occurred in held-out text — lower perplexity means the true next tokens were assigned higher probability on average, nothing more. It says nothing definitive about model size (A) or training data volume (D), both of which are confounded with many other factors, and factual accuracy (C) is a separate property perplexity doesn't directly measure — a model can be well-calibrated statistically while still stating incorrect facts fluently.

mcqs.question: Model A (word-level tokenizer, 50k vocab) reports lower perplexity than Model B (subword tokenizer, 30k vocab) on the same corpus. Is it valid to conclude Model A is the better language model?
options: Yes, lower perplexity always means a strictly better model regardless of tokenizer

Not directly — perplexity is computed per token, and differing tokenizers/vocabularies change what counts as one token, so the comparison is confounded unless normalized (e.g. to bits-per-character) or computed under a shared tokenizer
No, because perplexity can only be compared between models of identical architecture
Yes, but only if both models were trained for the same number of epochs
mcqs.explanation: This is the exact pitfall: perplexity's per-token basis makes cross-tokenizer comparisons unreliable, since a larger, coarser vocabulary can yield lower perplexity per token without genuinely better language understanding — valid comparison requires a shared tokenizer or a token-independent normalization. It isn't a blanket rule that lower is always better across any setup (A), the constraint is about tokenizer/vocabulary, not architecture identity (C is too strict/wrong reason), and epoch count (D) is unrelated to this specific confound.

mcqs.question: A large pretrained language model, given only a few example input-output pairs in its prompt and no gradient updates, correctly performs a translation task it was never explicitly fine-tuned for. What is this capability called, and what enabled it?
options: Transfer learning via fine-tuning — the model's weights were updated on translation examples
Few-shot learning — an emergent capability that appears at sufficient model and data scale, letting next-token prediction alone generalize to tasks never explicitly trained for
This is impossible without task-specific supervised training; the example must involve some fine-tuning
This only works because the model has internet access at inference time
mcqs.explanation: This describes few-shot (in-context) learning: no weights are updated, the model performs the task purely from the pattern shown in the prompt, and this ability to generalize beyond explicit training emerges at large enough scale. It's explicitly not fine-tuning, since no gradient updates occur (A is wrong), it genuinely happens without task-specific supervised training given sufficient scale (C is false), and it requires no internet access — it's a property of the pretrained weights and the prompt alone (D is false).
